lesson.title: Completing the Set: The Derivative of Cosecant
lesson.summary: Cosecant mirrors secant exactly, with sine replacing cosine, so the same reciprocal rule argument that produced sec x tan x now produces negative csc x cot x, closing out the six trigonometric derivatives.
lesson.body:
Cosecant is defined as csc x = 1/sin x, and after just finding the derivative of secant, which was built the same way from 1/cos x, this derivation should feel familiar rather than new. The parallel is intentional: secant and cosecant are mirror images of each other, one built from cosine and one from sine, and their derivatives will turn out to be mirror images too.

Apply the reciprocal rule to csc x = 1/sin x with g(x) = sin x, so g'(x) = cos x. The reciprocal rule gives d/dx[1/g(x)] = -g'(x)/[g(x)]^2 = -cos x/sin^2 x. Splitting this fraction as -(1/sin x)(cos x/sin x), and recognizing 1/sin x as csc x and cos x/sin x as cot x, gives the compact result d/dx csc x = -csc x cot x. The full quotient rule, applied to csc x = 1/sin x with f(x)=1, f'(x)=0, g(x)=sin x, g'(x)=cos x, gives the same [0*sin x - 1*cos x]/sin^2 x = -cos x/sin^2 x, confirming the answer through a second route.

Comparing this to the secant result from just before is instructive: d/dx sec x = sec x tan x has a positive sign, while d/dx csc x = -csc x cot x has a negative sign. This is not an inconsistency, it reflects genuine differences between how sine and cosine behave, particularly the extra minus sign that appears in d/dx sin x versus d/dx cos x = -sin x, which is exactly where the sign difference between these two final results originates.

A worked example at x = pi/6 checks the formula. sin(pi/6) = 0.5, so csc(pi/6) = 1/0.5 = 2. cos(pi/6) is about 0.86603, so cot(pi/6) = cos(pi/6)/sin(pi/6) = 0.86603/0.5, about 1.73206. The formula predicts csc'(pi/6) = -csc(pi/6)*cot(pi/6) = -2*1.73206, about -3.4641, which is exactly negative 2*sqrt(3).

The same kind of local extremum reasoning used for secant applies here too, shifted by a quarter turn. Sine reaches its maximum value of 1 at x = pi/2, so cosecant, being 1/sin x, reaches a minimum there instead. At exactly x = pi/2, csc(pi/2) = 1 and cot(pi/2) = cos(pi/2)/sin(pi/2) = 0/1 = 0, so the derivative -csc(pi/2)cot(pi/2) is 0, correctly flagging that minimum as a flat point on the graph, the same pattern that showed up for secant at x = 0.

A numerical check confirms this. Using the angle addition formula, sin(pi/6+0.001) = sin(pi/6)cos(0.001) + cos(pi/6)sin(0.001), about 0.5(0.9999995) + 0.86603(0.001), which comes to about 0.5008658. So csc(pi/6+0.001) = 1/0.5008658, about 1.996544. Since csc(pi/6) = 2, the difference quotient [1.996544 - 2]/0.001 is about -3.456, matching the predicted -3.4641 reasonably closely. As a final domain check, csc x is undefined wherever sin x = 0, and -csc x cot x is undefined at exactly those same points, since csc x = 1/sin x and cot x = cos x/sin x both involve dividing by sin x directly. With sine, cosine, tangent, cotangent, secant, and cosecant all now differentiated, and each one built from the last using the product, quotient, and reciprocal rules rather than six separate limit computations, the full set of trigonometric derivatives is complete and internally consistent.
